content: The deployment of community first responders (CFRs) to the scene of an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been proposed as a strategy to reduce the time between the onset of cardiac arrest and the initiation of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and defibrillation. This approach aims to improve survival rates among patients experiencing OHCA. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of mobilizing CFRs on survival outcomes and neurological function in adults and children older than four weeks of age. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted in January 2019 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science. Additional searches were performed in the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov. Abstracts from conferences held by the American Heart Association and the European Resuscitation Council were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials (q-RCTs) that compared standard emergency medical services (EMS) care with EMS care supplemented by CFR mobilization. Studies involving opportunistic bystanders or interventions targeting specific conditions, such as naloxone administration for opioid overdose, were excluded. The review included adults and children older than four weeks who experienced OHCA. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility of studies based on predefined criteria. Full-text articles of potentially relevant studies were obtained and examined in detail. Data extraction was performed independently by three reviewers using a standardized form, and the validity of each included trial was assessed using the Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Due to heterogeneity in the included studies, findings were synthesized narratively rather than through meta-analysis. The GRADE system was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence and to create a 'Summary of findings' table. Two completed studies, involving a total of 1,136 participants, met the inclusion criteria. One study was conducted in Amsterdam and surrounding areas between January 2000 and January 2002. This cluster-randomized trial evaluated the dispatch of police and fire service CFRs equipped with automated external defibrillators (AEDs). The study included adults aged 18 years or older who experienced witnessed OHCA. The results showed no significant difference in survival to hospital discharge between the intervention and control groups (odds ratio [OR] 1.3, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.8 to 2.2; low-certainty evidence). However, all 72 instances of defibrillation performed before EMS arrival occurred in the intervention group (moderate-certainty evidence). The study also reported increased survival to hospital admission in the intervention group (OR 1.5, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.0; moderate-certainty evidence). The second study was conducted in Stockholm, Sweden, between April 2012 and December 2013. This RCT evaluated the dispatch of nearby lay volunteers trained in CPR as a supplementary intervention in an EMS system where police and fire services were already routinely dispatched to OHCA events. The study included both witnessed and unwitnessed OHCA cases involving adults and children aged eight years or older. The results showed no significant difference in 30-day survival between the intervention and control groups (OR 1.34, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.29; low-certainty evidence). However, there was a significant increase in the performance of CPR before EMS arrival in the intervention group (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.03; moderate-certainty evidence). Neither of the included studies assessed neurological outcomes at hospital discharge or 30 days, nor did they evaluate health-related quality of life. The overall certainty of the evidence for the outcomes assessed was rated as low to moderate. The authors concluded that moderate-certainty evidence suggests that context-specific CFR interventions can increase the likelihood of CPR or defibrillation being performed before EMS arrival. However, it remains uncertain whether these interventions lead to significant improvements in overall survival rates. Further high-quality RCTs with sufficient power to detect changes in survival outcomes are needed. Additionally, future studies should routinely assess survival with good neurological function, as this outcome is likely to be of critical importance to patients. One ongoing study and one planned trial were identified, and their results may influence the findings of this review. The limitation of this review to randomized and quasi-randomized trials may have excluded relevant data from other study designs.
